Saigō Torizō (son) | relations = {{unbulleted list|Saigō Kichibei (father)|Shiihara Masa (mother)|{{ill|Saigō Jūdō|en|Saigō Jūdō|WD=Q699674|lt=Saigō Jūdō|1=Saigō Jūdō}} (brother)|Saigō Kichijirō (brother)|Saigō Kohei (brother)|Ichiki Koto (sister)|Saigō Taka (sister)|Saigō Yasu (sister)}} | laterwork = | signature = | signature_size = | signature_alt = | website = }} {{Nihongo|'''Saigō Takamori''' (or '''Takanaga''')|西鄕 隆盛 [隆永]|extra=January 23, 1828 – September 24, 1877}} was a Japanese {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} and nobleman. He was one of the most influential samurai in {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history|1=History of Japan}} and one of the {{ill|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|en|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|WD=Q709678|lt=three great nobles|1=Three Great Nobles of the Restoration}} who led the [[Meiji Restoration]]. Living during the late {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo|1=Edo period}} and early {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}s, he later led the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|en|Satsuma Rebellion|WD=Q714820|lt=Satsuma Rebellion|1=Satsuma Rebellion}} against the Meiji government. Historian {{ill|Ivan Morris|en|Ivan Morris|WD=Q3826587|lt=Ivan Morris|1=Ivan Morris}} described him as "the quintessential hero of modern Japanese history".{{Cite web|last=Hoffman|first=Michael|date=December 10, 2016|title=Meiji Restoration leader's lessons of sincerity|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2016/12/10/national/history/meiji-restoration-leaders-lessons-sincerity/|url-access=subscription|access-date=June 29, 2021|website=The Japan Times|language=en-US}} ==Early life== '''Saigō Kokichi''' (西郷 小吉) was born in Kajiya, {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain|1=Satsuma Domain}}, the eldest son of {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} {{ill|squire|en|squire|WD=Q579516|lt=squire|1=Squire}} (''koshōkumi'') Saigō Kichibē and his wife Masa.{{Cite book |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/33014222 |title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten |publisher=Asahi Shinbunsha |others=Asahi Shinbunsha, 朝日新聞社. |year=1994 |isbn=4-02-340052-1 |at=西郷隆盛 |oclc=33014222}} He had six siblings and his younger brother was {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|WD=Q121334120|lt=Marshal-Admiral|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)}} [[:en:Marquis|Marquis]] {{ill|Saigō Jūdō|en|Saigō Jūdō|WD=Q699674|lt=Saigō Jūdō|1=Saigō Jūdō}}. His childhood name was Kokichi and he received the given name Takamori in adulthood. He wrote poetry under the name '''Saigō Nanshū''' (西郷 南洲).Ravina, Mark. ''The Last Samurai: The Life and Battles of Saigō Takamori''. [[:en:John Wiley and Sons|John Wiley and Sons]], 2011. [https://books.google.com/books?id=lwt587Ex_a4C&pg=PT7 Names, Romanizations, and Spelling (page 1 of 2)]. Retrieved from {{ill|Google Books|en|Google Books|WD=Q206033|lt=Google Books|1=Google Books}} on August 7, 2011. {{ISBN|1-118-04556-4}}, {{ISBN|978-1-118-04556-5}}. Shogun [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] resigned, returning power to the Emperor in what came to be known as the [[Meiji Restoration]]. However, Saigō was one of the most vocal and vehement opponents to the negotiated solution, demanding that the Tokugawa be stripped of their lands and special status. His intransigence was one of the major causes of the subsequent {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}. During the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}, Saigō led the imperial forces at the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}}, and afterwards led the imperial army toward Edo, where he accepted the surrender of Edo Castle from {{ill|Katsu Kaishū|en|Katsu Kaishū|WD=Q700470|lt=Katsu Kaishū|1=Katsu Kaishū}}. ==Meiji bureaucrat== [[File:1873_Seikanron_Debate_Saigo_Takamori_Ukiyo-e_by_Suzuki_Toshimoto.png|thumb|left|The {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate. Saigō Takamori is sitting in the center. 1877 woodblock print]] Although {{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|WD=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}} and others were more active and influential in establishing the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Government of Meiji Japan|1=Government of Meiji Japan}}, Saigō retained a key role, and his cooperation was essential in the {{ill|Abolition of the han system|en|Abolition of the han system|WD=Q331905|lt=Abolition of the han system|1=Abolition of the han system}} and the establishment of a conscript army. In 1871 he was left in charge of the caretaker government during the absence of the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}} (1871–73). Saigō initially disagreed with the modernization of Japan and the opening of commerce with the West. He famously opposed the construction of a railway network, insisting that money should rather be spent on military modernization.{{Cite web |url=http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |title=On Saigō and the establishment of a railway |access-date=October 21, 2006 |archive-date=May 27, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527182301/http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |url-status=dead }} Saigō did insist that Japan should go to war with {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}} in the {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate of 1873 due to Korea's refusal to recognize the legitimacy of the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} as head of state of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}, and insulting treatment meted out to Japanese envoys attempting to establish trade and diplomatic relations. At one point, he offered to visit Korea in person and to provoke a ''{{ill|Casus belli|en|Casus belli|WD=Q45635|lt=Casus belli|1=Casus belli}}'' by behaving in such an insulting manner that the Koreans would be forced to kill him.{{Cite book |last=Ravina |first=Mark |title=The last Samurai - The life and Battles of Saigō Takamori |publisher=Wiley Online library |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-471-70537-6 |pages=184}} The other Japanese leaders strongly opposed these plans, partly from budgetary considerations, and partly from realization of the weakness of Japan compared with the western countries from what they had witnessed during the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}}. Saigō resigned from all of his government positions in protest and returned to his hometown of {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}. ==Satsuma Rebellion (1877)== {{Main|Satsuma Rebellion}} [[File:Saigo Takamori Portrait by Tokonami Masayoshi 1887.png|thumb|Portrait of Saigō Takamori as a {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|WD=Q3100832|lt=field marshal|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)}}, faithful depiction by the acquaintance Tokonami Masayoshi in 1887]] [[File:Seinansenso snou.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō preparing for war]] Shortly thereafter, a private military academy known as the {{ill|Shi-gakkō|en|Shi-gakkō|WD=Q11594685|lt=Shi-gakkō|1=Shi-gakkō}} was established in Kagoshima for the faithful ''samurai'' who had also resigned their posts to follow him from Tokyo. These disaffected samurai came to dominate the Kagoshima government, and fearing a rebellion, the government sent warships to Kagoshima to remove weapons from the Kagoshima arsenal. This provoked open conflict, although with the elimination of ''samurai'' rice stipends in 1877, tensions were already extremely high. Although greatly dismayed by the revolt, Saigō was reluctantly persuaded to lead the rebels against the central government. [[File:ShiroyamaBattle.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō Takamori (upper right) directing his troops at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}]] The rebels fought two significant battles against the central government: the {{ill|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|en|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|WD=Q7510168|lt=Siege of Kumamoto Castle|1=Siege of Kumamoto Castle}} and the {{ill|Battle of Tabaruzaka|en|Battle of Tabaruzaka|WD=Q9347968|lt=Battle of Tabaruzaka|1=Battle of Tabaruzaka}}. Saigō was initially confident of his ability to take Kumamoto Castle, but he had underestimated the effectiveness of the imperial conscripts defending the castle. After a failed assault, Saigō settled for a siege. Imperial reinforcements eventually forced their way through the rebel lines at the Battle of Tabaruzaka, ending the siege. The remnants of Saigō's army retreated before the advancing imperials, who whittled it down relentlessly. Eventually Saigō and his final remaining samurai were encircled and annihilated at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}. Saigō's death brought the Satsuma Rebellion to an end. ==Death== [[File:Saigo Takamori Woodblock Print Portrait by Hasegawa Sadanobu II 1877.png|thumb|Woodblock print of Saigō Takamori by Hasegawa Sadanobu II which describes his career, November 1877]] During the battle of Shiroyama, Saigō was badly injured in the hip. The exact manner of his death is unknown. There are no published reports by eyewitnesses. The accounts of his subordinates claim that he stood up and committed ''{{ill|Seppuku|en|Seppuku|WD=Q133462|lt=Seppuku|1=Seppuku}}'' after his injury or that he requested that his friend {{ill|Beppu Shinsuke|en|Beppu Shinsuke|WD=Q937740|lt=Beppu Shinsuke|1=Beppu Shinsuke}} assist his suicide. Three firsthand accounts of the condition of his deceased body exist. It is said that he was shot in the femur, then he thrust a sword into his stomach region, then was decapitated deliberately by a fellow citizen. All three accounts report that the body was decapitated. Two describe a bullet wound to the hip or thigh. As none of the eyewitness accounts mention a wound to the abdomen, or any fresh sword wound at all, it is unknown if Saigō pierced his stomach with his sword.Ravina, Mark J. “The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, Seppuku, and the Politics of Legend.” Journal of Asian Studies 69.3 (2010): 691-721. Some scholars have suggested that neither is the case and that Saigō may have gone into shock following his wound, losing his ability to speak. Several samurai, upon seeing him in this state, would have severed his head, assisting him in the warrior's suicide that they knew he would have wished for. Later, they would have said that he committed ''seppuku'' to preserve his status as a true ''samurai''.{{cite web |url=http://www.emory.edu/EMORY_MAGAZINE/spring2004/precis_samurai.html|title=The Real Last Samurai|publisher=Emory University |website=Emory Magazine|editor=Andrew M. Beierle|access-date=April 10, 2009}} It is not clear what was done with Saigō's head immediately after his death. Some legends say Saigō's manservant hid the head, and it was later found by a government soldier. The head was somehow retrieved by government forces and was reunited with Saigō's body, which was laid next to that of his deputies Kirino and Murata. This was witnessed by the American sea captain John Capen Hubbard. A myth persists that the head was never found. ==Legends== [[File:Saigo Takamori Gunmusho banknote 1877.jpg|thumb|150px|left|Saigō Takamori ''Gunmusho'' (軍務所) banknote, issued in 1877 to finance his war effort. [[:en:Japan Currency Museum|Japan Currency Museum]]]] Multiple legends sprang up concerning Saigō, many of which denied his death. It was believed by some that he had fled to {{ill|Russia|en|Russia|WD=Q159|lt=Russia|1=Russia}}, or ascended to {{ill|Mars|en|Mars|WD=Q111|lt=Mars|1=Mars}}.{{Cite journal|last=RAVINA|first=MARK J.|date=2010|title=The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, "Seppuku", and the Politics of Legend|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40929189|journal=The Journal of Asian Studies|volume=69|issue=3|pages=691–721|doi=10.1017/S0021911810001518|jstor=40929189|s2cid=155001706|issn=0021-9118}} It was even recorded that his image appeared in a comet near the close of the 19th century, an ill omen to his enemies. Unable to overcome the affection that the people had for this paragon of traditional ''samurai'' virtues, the [[:en:Meiji-era|Meiji-era]] government pardoned him posthumously on February 22, 1889. The Japanese people appreciated the fact that he remained loyal to his virtues until his death in 1877. ==Artworks depicting Saigō== [[File:Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku
(Gion, Kyoto, Japan)]] [[File:SaigoTakamori1332.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Saigō Takamori's statue near the southern entrance of Ueno Park.]] [[File:Deathplace of SAIGO Takamori.JPG|thumb|150px|The death place monument at Shiroyama-chō, Kagoshima]] Saigō famously refused to have his photograph taken, but his likeness is now highly visible in Tokyo. A famous bronze statue of Saigō in hunting attire with his dog stands in {{ill|Ueno Park|en|Ueno Park|WD=Q746216|lt=Ueno Park|1=Ueno Park}}, {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}. Made by {{ill|Takamura Kōun|en|Takamura Kōun|WD=Q2080344|lt=Takamura Kōun|1=Takamura Kōun}}, it was unveiled on December 18, 1898. Saigō met the noted British {{ill|Diplomat|en|Diplomat|WD=Q193391|lt=Diplomat|1=Diplomat}} [[:en:Ernest Satow|Ernest Satow]] in the 1860s, as recorded in the latter's ''A Diplomat in Japan'', and Satow was present at the unveiling as recorded in his diary. A reproduction of the same statue stands on {{ill|Okinoerabujima|en|Okinoerabujima|WD=Q94736|lt=Okinoerabujima|1=Okinoerabujima}}, where Saigō had been exiled.{{ill|John Man (author)|en|John Man (author)|WD=Q3431828|lt=Man, John|1=John Man (author)}}. "In the Footsteps of the Real Last Samurai." ''[[:en:School of Oriental and African Studies|SOAS]] World''. 37 (Spring 2011). p30. A Japanese hand fan commemorating the event, which survives in the collection of the Staten Island Historical Society in New York, features a depiction of Saigō Takamori in a scene labeled (in English) "The Battle Near the Citadel of Kumamoto".{{cite web|title=Fan, 1877–1890|url=https://statenisland.pastperfectonline.com/webobject/2BBDFB3D-A583-4BB0-AF0E-163644731340|website=Online Collections Database|publisher=Staten Island Historical Society|access-date=December 2, 2011}} ==Family== ===Ancestry=== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=no |align=center |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1. He was one of the most influential samurai in {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history|1=History of Japan}} and one of the {{ill|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|en|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|WD=Q709678|lt=three great nobles|1=Three Great Nobles of the Restoration}} who led the [[Meiji Restoration]]. Living during the late {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo|1=Edo period}} and early {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}s, he later led the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|en|Satsuma Rebellion|WD=Q714820|lt=Satsuma Rebellion|1=Satsuma Rebellion}} against the Meiji government. Historian {{ill|Ivan Morris|en|Ivan Morris|WD=Q3826587|lt=Ivan Morris|1=Ivan Morris}} described him as "the quintessential hero of modern Japanese history".{{Cite web|last=Hoffman|first=Michael|date=December 10, 2016|title=Meiji Restoration leader's lessons of sincerity|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2016/12/10/national/history/meiji-restoration-leaders-lessons-sincerity/|url-access=subscription|access-date=June 29, 2021|website=The Japan Times|language=en-US}} ==Early life== '''Saigō Kokichi''' (西郷 小吉) was born in Kajiya, {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain|1=Satsuma Domain}}, the eldest son of {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} {{ill|squire|en|squire|WD=Q579516|lt=squire|1=Squire}} (''koshōkumi'') Saigō Kichibē and his wife Masa.{{Cite book |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/33014222 |title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten |publisher=Asahi Shinbunsha |others=Asahi Shinbunsha, 朝日新聞社. |year=1994 |isbn=4-02-340052-1 |at=西郷隆盛 |oclc=33014222}} He had six siblings and his younger brother was {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|WD=Q121334120|lt=Marshal-Admiral|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)}} [[:en:Marquis|Marquis]] {{ill|Saigō Jūdō|en|Saigō Jūdō|WD=Q699674|lt=Saigō Jūdō|1=Saigō Jūdō}}. His childhood name was Kokichi and he received the given name Takamori in adulthood. He wrote poetry under the name '''Saigō Nanshū''' (西郷 南洲).Ravina, Mark. ''The Last Samurai: The Life and Battles of Saigō Takamori''. [[:en:John Wiley and Sons|John Wiley and Sons]], 2011. [https://books.google.com/books?id=lwt587Ex_a4C&pg=PT7 Names, Romanizations, and Spelling (page 1 of 2)]. Retrieved from {{ill|Google Books|en|Google Books|WD=Q206033|lt=Google Books|1=Google Books}} on August 7, 2011. {{ISBN|1-118-04556-4}}, {{ISBN|978-1-118-04556-5}}. Shogun [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] resigned, returning power to the Emperor in what came to be known as the [[Meiji Restoration]]. However, Saigō was one of the most vocal and vehement opponents to the negotiated solution, demanding that the Tokugawa be stripped of their lands and special status. His intransigence was one of the major causes of the subsequent {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}. During the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}, Saigō led the imperial forces at the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}}, and afterwards led the imperial army toward Edo, where he accepted the surrender of Edo Castle from {{ill|Katsu Kaishū|en|Katsu Kaishū|WD=Q700470|lt=Katsu Kaishū|1=Katsu Kaishū}}. ==Meiji bureaucrat== [[File:1873_Seikanron_Debate_Saigo_Takamori_Ukiyo-e_by_Suzuki_Toshimoto.png|thumb|left|The {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate. Saigō Takamori is sitting in the center. 1877 woodblock print]] Although {{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|WD=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}} and others were more active and influential in establishing the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Government of Meiji Japan|1=Government of Meiji Japan}}, Saigō retained a key role, and his cooperation was essential in the {{ill|Abolition of the han system|en|Abolition of the han system|WD=Q331905|lt=Abolition of the han system|1=Abolition of the han system}} and the establishment of a conscript army. In 1871 he was left in charge of the caretaker government during the absence of the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}} (1871–73). Saigō initially disagreed with the modernization of Japan and the opening of commerce with the West. He famously opposed the construction of a railway network, insisting that money should rather be spent on military modernization.{{Cite web |url=http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |title=On Saigō and the establishment of a railway |access-date=October 21, 2006 |archive-date=May 27, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527182301/http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |url-status=dead }} Saigō did insist that Japan should go to war with {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}} in the {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate of 1873 due to Korea's refusal to recognize the legitimacy of the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} as head of state of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}, and insulting treatment meted out to Japanese envoys attempting to establish trade and diplomatic relations. At one point, he offered to visit Korea in person and to provoke a ''{{ill|Casus belli|en|Casus belli|WD=Q45635|lt=Casus belli|1=Casus belli}}'' by behaving in such an insulting manner that the Koreans would be forced to kill him.{{Cite book |last=Ravina |first=Mark |title=The last Samurai - The life and Battles of Saigō Takamori |publisher=Wiley Online library |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-471-70537-6 |pages=184}} The other Japanese leaders strongly opposed these plans, partly from budgetary considerations, and partly from realization of the weakness of Japan compared with the western countries from what they had witnessed during the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}}. Saigō resigned from all of his government positions in protest and returned to his hometown of {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}. ==Satsuma Rebellion (1877)== {{Main|Satsuma Rebellion}} [[File:Saigo Takamori Portrait by Tokonami Masayoshi 1887.png|thumb|Portrait of Saigō Takamori as a {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|WD=Q3100832|lt=field marshal|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)}}, faithful depiction by the acquaintance Tokonami Masayoshi in 1887]] [[File:Seinansenso snou.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō preparing for war]] Shortly thereafter, a private military academy known as the {{ill|Shi-gakkō|en|Shi-gakkō|WD=Q11594685|lt=Shi-gakkō|1=Shi-gakkō}} was established in Kagoshima for the faithful ''samurai'' who had also resigned their posts to follow him from Tokyo. These disaffected samurai came to dominate the Kagoshima government, and fearing a rebellion, the government sent warships to Kagoshima to remove weapons from the Kagoshima arsenal. This provoked open conflict, although with the elimination of ''samurai'' rice stipends in 1877, tensions were already extremely high. Although greatly dismayed by the revolt, Saigō was reluctantly persuaded to lead the rebels against the central government. [[File:ShiroyamaBattle.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō Takamori (upper right) directing his troops at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}]] The rebels fought two significant battles against the central government: the {{ill|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|en|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|WD=Q7510168|lt=Siege of Kumamoto Castle|1=Siege of Kumamoto Castle}} and the {{ill|Battle of Tabaruzaka|en|Battle of Tabaruzaka|WD=Q9347968|lt=Battle of Tabaruzaka|1=Battle of Tabaruzaka}}. Saigō was initially confident of his ability to take Kumamoto Castle, but he had underestimated the effectiveness of the imperial conscripts defending the castle. After a failed assault, Saigō settled for a siege. Imperial reinforcements eventually forced their way through the rebel lines at the Battle of Tabaruzaka, ending the siege. The remnants of Saigō's army retreated before the advancing imperials, who whittled it down relentlessly. Eventually Saigō and his final remaining samurai were encircled and annihilated at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}. Saigō's death brought the Satsuma Rebellion to an end. ==Death== [[File:Saigo Takamori Woodblock Print Portrait by Hasegawa Sadanobu II 1877.png|thumb|Woodblock print of Saigō Takamori by Hasegawa Sadanobu II which describes his career, November 1877]] During the battle of Shiroyama, Saigō was badly injured in the hip. The exact manner of his death is unknown. There are no published reports by eyewitnesses. The accounts of his subordinates claim that he stood up and committed ''{{ill|Seppuku|en|Seppuku|WD=Q133462|lt=Seppuku|1=Seppuku}}'' after his injury or that he requested that his friend {{ill|Beppu Shinsuke|en|Beppu Shinsuke|WD=Q937740|lt=Beppu Shinsuke|1=Beppu Shinsuke}} assist his suicide. Three firsthand accounts of the condition of his deceased body exist. It is said that he was shot in the femur, then he thrust a sword into his stomach region, then was decapitated deliberately by a fellow citizen. All three accounts report that the body was decapitated. Two describe a bullet wound to the hip or thigh. As none of the eyewitness accounts mention a wound to the abdomen, or any fresh sword wound at all, it is unknown if Saigō pierced his stomach with his sword.Ravina, Mark J. “The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, Seppuku, and the Politics of Legend.” Journal of Asian Studies 69.3 (2010): 691-721. Some scholars have suggested that neither is the case and that Saigō may have gone into shock following his wound, losing his ability to speak. Several samurai, upon seeing him in this state, would have severed his head, assisting him in the warrior's suicide that they knew he would have wished for. Later, they would have said that he committed ''seppuku'' to preserve his status as a true ''samurai''.{{cite web |url=http://www.emory.edu/EMORY_MAGAZINE/spring2004/precis_samurai.html|title=The Real Last Samurai|publisher=Emory University |website=Emory Magazine|editor=Andrew M. Beierle|access-date=April 10, 2009}} It is not clear what was done with Saigō's head immediately after his death. Some legends say Saigō's manservant hid the head, and it was later found by a government soldier. The head was somehow retrieved by government forces and was reunited with Saigō's body, which was laid next to that of his deputies Kirino and Murata. This was witnessed by the American sea captain John Capen Hubbard. A myth persists that the head was never found. ==Legends== [[File:Saigo Takamori Gunmusho banknote 1877.jpg|thumb|150px|left|Saigō Takamori ''Gunmusho'' (軍務所) banknote, issued in 1877 to finance his war effort. [[:en:Japan Currency Museum|Japan Currency Museum]]]] Multiple legends sprang up concerning Saigō, many of which denied his death. It was believed by some that he had fled to {{ill|Russia|en|Russia|WD=Q159|lt=Russia|1=Russia}}, or ascended to {{ill|Mars|en|Mars|WD=Q111|lt=Mars|1=Mars}}.{{Cite journal|last=RAVINA|first=MARK J.|date=2010|title=The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, "Seppuku", and the Politics of Legend|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40929189|journal=The Journal of Asian Studies|volume=69|issue=3|pages=691–721|doi=10.1017/S0021911810001518|jstor=40929189|s2cid=155001706|issn=0021-9118}} It was even recorded that his image appeared in a comet near the close of the 19th century, an ill omen to his enemies. Unable to overcome the affection that the people had for this paragon of traditional ''samurai'' virtues, the [[:en:Meiji-era|Meiji-era]] government pardoned him posthumously on February 22, 1889. The Japanese people appreciated the fact that he remained loyal to his virtues until his death in 1877. ==Artworks depicting Saigō== [[File:Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku
(Gion, Kyoto, Japan)]] [[File:SaigoTakamori1332.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Saigō Takamori's statue near the southern entrance of Ueno Park.]] [[File:Deathplace of SAIGO Takamori.JPG|thumb|150px|The death place monument at Shiroyama-chō, Kagoshima]] Saigō famously refused to have his photograph taken, but his likeness is now highly visible in Tokyo. A famous bronze statue of Saigō in hunting attire with his dog stands in {{ill|Ueno Park|en|Ueno Park|WD=Q746216|lt=Ueno Park|1=Ueno Park}}, {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}. Made by {{ill|Takamura Kōun|en|Takamura Kōun|WD=Q2080344|lt=Takamura Kōun|1=Takamura Kōun}}, it was unveiled on December 18, 1898. Saigō met the noted British {{ill|Diplomat|en|Diplomat|WD=Q193391|lt=Diplomat|1=Diplomat}} [[:en:Ernest Satow|Ernest Satow]] in the 1860s, as recorded in the latter's ''A Diplomat in Japan'', and Satow was present at the unveiling as recorded in his diary. A reproduction of the same statue stands on {{ill|Okinoerabujima|en|Okinoerabujima|WD=Q94736|lt=Okinoerabujima|1=Okinoerabujima}}, where Saigō had been exiled.{{ill|John Man (author)|en|John Man (author)|WD=Q3431828|lt=Man, John|1=John Man (author)}}. "In the Footsteps of the Real Last Samurai." ''[[:en:School of Oriental and African Studies|SOAS]] World''. 37 (Spring 2011). p30. A Japanese hand fan commemorating the event, which survives in the collection of the Staten Island Historical Society in New York, features a depiction of Saigō Takamori in a scene labeled (in English) "The Battle Near the Citadel of Kumamoto".{{cite web|title=Fan, 1877–1890|url=https://statenisland.pastperfectonline.com/webobject/2BBDFB3D-A583-4BB0-AF0E-163644731340|website=Online Collections Database|publisher=Staten Island Historical Society|access-date=December 2, 2011}} ==Family== ===Ancestry=== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=no |align=center |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1. Saigō Torizō (son) | relations = {{unbulleted list|Saigō Kichibei (father)|Shiihara Masa (mother)|{{ill|Saigō Jūdō|en|Saigō Jūdō|WD=Q699674|lt=Saigō Jūdō|1=Saigō Jūdō}} (brother)|Saigō Kichijirō (brother)|Saigō Kohei (brother)|Ichiki Koto (sister)|Saigō Taka (sister)|Saigō Yasu (sister)}} | laterwork = | signature = | signature_size = | signature_alt = | website = }} {{Nihongo|'''Saigō Takamori''' (or '''Takanaga''')|西鄕 隆盛 [隆永]|extra=January 23, 1828 – September 24, 1877}} was a Japanese {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} and nobleman. He was one of the most influential samurai in {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history|1=History of Japan}} and one of the {{ill|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|en|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|WD=Q709678|lt=three great nobles|1=Three Great Nobles of the Restoration}} who led the [[Meiji Restoration]]. Living during the late {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo|1=Edo period}} and early {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}s, he later led the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|en|Satsuma Rebellion|WD=Q714820|lt=Satsuma Rebellion|1=Satsuma Rebellion}} against the Meiji government. Historian {{ill|Ivan Morris|en|Ivan Morris|WD=Q3826587|lt=Ivan Morris|1=Ivan Morris}} described him as "the quintessential hero of modern Japanese history".{{Cite web|last=Hoffman|first=Michael|date=December 10, 2016|title=Meiji Restoration leader's lessons of sincerity|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2016/12/10/national/history/meiji-restoration-leaders-lessons-sincerity/|url-access=subscription|access-date=June 29, 2021|website=The Japan Times|language=en-US}} ==Early life== '''Saigō Kokichi''' (西郷 小吉) was born in Kajiya, {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain|1=Satsuma Domain}}, the eldest son of {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} {{ill|squire|en|squire|WD=Q579516|lt=squire|1=Squire}} (''koshōkumi'') Saigō Kichibē and his wife Masa.{{Cite book |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/33014222 |title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten |publisher=Asahi Shinbunsha |others=Asahi Shinbunsha, 朝日新聞社. |year=1994 |isbn=4-02-340052-1 |at=西郷隆盛 |oclc=33014222}} He had six siblings and his younger brother was {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|WD=Q121334120|lt=Marshal-Admiral|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)}} [[:en:Marquis|Marquis]] {{ill|Saigō Jūdō|en|Saigō Jūdō|WD=Q699674|lt=Saigō Jūdō|1=Saigō Jūdō}}. His childhood name was Kokichi and he received the given name Takamori in adulthood. He wrote poetry under the name '''Saigō Nanshū''' (西郷 南洲).Ravina, Mark. ''The Last Samurai: The Life and Battles of Saigō Takamori''. [[:en:John Wiley and Sons|John Wiley and Sons]], 2011. [https://books.google.com/books?id=lwt587Ex_a4C&pg=PT7 Names, Romanizations, and Spelling (page 1 of 2)]. Retrieved from {{ill|Google Books|en|Google Books|WD=Q206033|lt=Google Books|1=Google Books}} on August 7, 2011. {{ISBN|1-118-04556-4}}, {{ISBN|978-1-118-04556-5}}. Shogun [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] resigned, returning power to the Emperor in what came to be known as the [[Meiji Restoration]]. However, Saigō was one of the most vocal and vehement opponents to the negotiated solution, demanding that the Tokugawa be stripped of their lands and special status. His intransigence was one of the major causes of the subsequent {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}. During the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}, Saigō led the imperial forces at the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}}, and afterwards led the imperial army toward Edo, where he accepted the surrender of Edo Castle from {{ill|Katsu Kaishū|en|Katsu Kaishū|WD=Q700470|lt=Katsu Kaishū|1=Katsu Kaishū}}. ==Meiji bureaucrat== [[File:1873_Seikanron_Debate_Saigo_Takamori_Ukiyo-e_by_Suzuki_Toshimoto.png|thumb|left|The {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate. Saigō Takamori is sitting in the center. 1877 woodblock print]] Although {{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|WD=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}} and others were more active and influential in establishing the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Government of Meiji Japan|1=Government of Meiji Japan}}, Saigō retained a key role, and his cooperation was essential in the {{ill|Abolition of the han system|en|Abolition of the han system|WD=Q331905|lt=Abolition of the han system|1=Abolition of the han system}} and the establishment of a conscript army. In 1871 he was left in charge of the caretaker government during the absence of the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}} (1871–73). Saigō initially disagreed with the modernization of Japan and the opening of commerce with the West. He famously opposed the construction of a railway network, insisting that money should rather be spent on military modernization.{{Cite web |url=http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |title=On Saigō and the establishment of a railway |access-date=October 21, 2006 |archive-date=May 27, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527182301/http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |url-status=dead }} Saigō did insist that Japan should go to war with {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}} in the {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate of 1873 due to Korea's refusal to recognize the legitimacy of the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} as head of state of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}, and insulting treatment meted out to Japanese envoys attempting to establish trade and diplomatic relations. At one point, he offered to visit Korea in person and to provoke a ''{{ill|Casus belli|en|Casus belli|WD=Q45635|lt=Casus belli|1=Casus belli}}'' by behaving in such an insulting manner that the Koreans would be forced to kill him.{{Cite book |last=Ravina |first=Mark |title=The last Samurai - The life and Battles of Saigō Takamori |publisher=Wiley Online library |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-471-70537-6 |pages=184}} The other Japanese leaders strongly opposed these plans, partly from budgetary considerations, and partly from realization of the weakness of Japan compared with the western countries from what they had witnessed during the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}}. Saigō resigned from all of his government positions in protest and returned to his hometown of {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}. ==Satsuma Rebellion (1877)== {{Main|Satsuma Rebellion}} [[File:Saigo Takamori Portrait by Tokonami Masayoshi 1887.png|thumb|Portrait of Saigō Takamori as a {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|WD=Q3100832|lt=field marshal|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)}}, faithful depiction by the acquaintance Tokonami Masayoshi in 1887]] [[File:Seinansenso snou.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō preparing for war]] Shortly thereafter, a private military academy known as the {{ill|Shi-gakkō|en|Shi-gakkō|WD=Q11594685|lt=Shi-gakkō|1=Shi-gakkō}} was established in Kagoshima for the faithful ''samurai'' who had also resigned their posts to follow him from Tokyo. These disaffected samurai came to dominate the Kagoshima government, and fearing a rebellion, the government sent warships to Kagoshima to remove weapons from the Kagoshima arsenal. This provoked open conflict, although with the elimination of ''samurai'' rice stipends in 1877, tensions were already extremely high. Although greatly dismayed by the revolt, Saigō was reluctantly persuaded to lead the rebels against the central government. [[File:ShiroyamaBattle.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō Takamori (upper right) directing his troops at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}]] The rebels fought two significant battles against the central government: the {{ill|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|en|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|WD=Q7510168|lt=Siege of Kumamoto Castle|1=Siege of Kumamoto Castle}} and the {{ill|Battle of Tabaruzaka|en|Battle of Tabaruzaka|WD=Q9347968|lt=Battle of Tabaruzaka|1=Battle of Tabaruzaka}}. Saigō was initially confident of his ability to take Kumamoto Castle, but he had underestimated the effectiveness of the imperial conscripts defending the castle. After a failed assault, Saigō settled for a siege. Imperial reinforcements eventually forced their way through the rebel lines at the Battle of Tabaruzaka, ending the siege. The remnants of Saigō's army retreated before the advancing imperials, who whittled it down relentlessly. Eventually Saigō and his final remaining samurai were encircled and annihilated at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}. Saigō's death brought the Satsuma Rebellion to an end. ==Death== [[File:Saigo Takamori Woodblock Print Portrait by Hasegawa Sadanobu II 1877.png|thumb|Woodblock print of Saigō Takamori by Hasegawa Sadanobu II which describes his career, November 1877]] During the battle of Shiroyama, Saigō was badly injured in the hip. The exact manner of his death is unknown. There are no published reports by eyewitnesses. The accounts of his subordinates claim that he stood up and committed ''{{ill|Seppuku|en|Seppuku|WD=Q133462|lt=Seppuku|1=Seppuku}}'' after his injury or that he requested that his friend {{ill|Beppu Shinsuke|en|Beppu Shinsuke|WD=Q937740|lt=Beppu Shinsuke|1=Beppu Shinsuke}} assist his suicide. Three firsthand accounts of the condition of his deceased body exist. It is said that he was shot in the femur, then he thrust a sword into his stomach region, then was decapitated deliberately by a fellow citizen. All three accounts report that the body was decapitated. Two describe a bullet wound to the hip or thigh. As none of the eyewitness accounts mention a wound to the abdomen, or any fresh sword wound at all, it is unknown if Saigō pierced his stomach with his sword.Ravina, Mark J. “The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, Seppuku, and the Politics of Legend.” Journal of Asian Studies 69.3 (2010): 691-721. Some scholars have suggested that neither is the case and that Saigō may have gone into shock following his wound, losing his ability to speak. Several samurai, upon seeing him in this state, would have severed his head, assisting him in the warrior's suicide that they knew he would have wished for. Later, they would have said that he committed ''seppuku'' to preserve his status as a true ''samurai''.{{cite web |url=http://www.emory.edu/EMORY_MAGAZINE/spring2004/precis_samurai.html|title=The Real Last Samurai|publisher=Emory University |website=Emory Magazine|editor=Andrew M. Beierle|access-date=April 10, 2009}} It is not clear what was done with Saigō's head immediately after his death. Some legends say Saigō's manservant hid the head, and it was later found by a government soldier. The head was somehow retrieved by government forces and was reunited with Saigō's body, which was laid next to that of his deputies Kirino and Murata. This was witnessed by the American sea captain John Capen Hubbard. A myth persists that the head was never found. ==Legends== [[File:Saigo Takamori Gunmusho banknote 1877.jpg|thumb|150px|left|Saigō Takamori ''Gunmusho'' (軍務所) banknote, issued in 1877 to finance his war effort. [[:en:Japan Currency Museum|Japan Currency Museum]]]] Multiple legends sprang up concerning Saigō, many of which denied his death. It was believed by some that he had fled to {{ill|Russia|en|Russia|WD=Q159|lt=Russia|1=Russia}}, or ascended to {{ill|Mars|en|Mars|WD=Q111|lt=Mars|1=Mars}}.{{Cite journal|last=RAVINA|first=MARK J.|date=2010|title=The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, "Seppuku", and the Politics of Legend|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40929189|journal=The Journal of Asian Studies|volume=69|issue=3|pages=691–721|doi=10.1017/S0021911810001518|jstor=40929189|s2cid=155001706|issn=0021-9118}} It was even recorded that his image appeared in a comet near the close of the 19th century, an ill omen to his enemies. Unable to overcome the affection that the people had for this paragon of traditional ''samurai'' virtues, the [[:en:Meiji-era|Meiji-era]] government pardoned him posthumously on February 22, 1889. The Japanese people appreciated the fact that he remained loyal to his virtues until his death in 1877. ==Artworks depicting Saigō== [[File:Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku
(Gion, Kyoto, Japan)]] [[File:SaigoTakamori1332.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Saigō Takamori's statue near the southern entrance of Ueno Park.]] [[File:Deathplace of SAIGO Takamori.JPG|thumb|150px|The death place monument at Shiroyama-chō, Kagoshima]] Saigō famously refused to have his photograph taken, but his likeness is now highly visible in Tokyo. A famous bronze statue of Saigō in hunting attire with his dog stands in {{ill|Ueno Park|en|Ueno Park|WD=Q746216|lt=Ueno Park|1=Ueno Park}}, {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}. Made by {{ill|Takamura Kōun|en|Takamura Kōun|WD=Q2080344|lt=Takamura Kōun|1=Takamura Kōun}}, it was unveiled on December 18, 1898. Saigō met the noted British {{ill|Diplomat|en|Diplomat|WD=Q193391|lt=Diplomat|1=Diplomat}} [[:en:Ernest Satow|Ernest Satow]] in the 1860s, as recorded in the latter's ''A Diplomat in Japan'', and Satow was present at the unveiling as recorded in his diary. A reproduction of the same statue stands on {{ill|Okinoerabujima|en|Okinoerabujima|WD=Q94736|lt=Okinoerabujima|1=Okinoerabujima}}, where Saigō had been exiled.{{ill|John Man (author)|en|John Man (author)|WD=Q3431828|lt=Man, John|1=John Man (author)}}. "In the Footsteps of the Real Last Samurai." ''[[:en:School of Oriental and African Studies|SOAS]] World''. 37 (Spring 2011). p30. A Japanese hand fan commemorating the event, which survives in the collection of the Staten Island Historical Society in New York, features a depiction of Saigō Takamori in a scene labeled (in English) "The Battle Near the Citadel of Kumamoto".{{cite web|title=Fan, 1877–1890|url=https://statenisland.pastperfectonline.com/webobject/2BBDFB3D-A583-4BB0-AF0E-163644731340|website=Online Collections Database|publisher=Staten Island Historical Society|access-date=December 2, 2011}} ==Family== ===Ancestry=== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=no |align=center |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1. He was one of the most influential samurai in {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history|1=History of Japan}} and one of the {{ill|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|en|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|WD=Q709678|lt=three great nobles|1=Three Great Nobles of the Restoration}} who led the [[Meiji Restoration]]. Living during the late {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo|1=Edo period}} and early {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}s, he later led the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|en|Satsuma Rebellion|WD=Q714820|lt=Satsuma Rebellion|1=Satsuma Rebellion}} against the Meiji government. Historian {{ill|Ivan Morris|en|Ivan Morris|WD=Q3826587|lt=Ivan Morris|1=Ivan Morris}} described him as "the quintessential hero of modern Japanese history".{{Cite web|last=Hoffman|first=Michael|date=December 10, 2016|title=Meiji Restoration leader's lessons of sincerity|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2016/12/10/national/history/meiji-restoration-leaders-lessons-sincerity/|url-access=subscription|access-date=June 29, 2021|website=The Japan Times|language=en-US}} ==Early life== '''Saigō Kokichi''' (西郷 小吉) was born in Kajiya, {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain|1=Satsuma Domain}}, the eldest son of {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} {{ill|squire|en|squire|WD=Q579516|lt=squire|1=Squire}} (''koshōkumi'') Saigō Kichibē and his wife Masa.{{Cite book |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/33014222 |title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten |publisher=Asahi Shinbunsha |others=Asahi Shinbunsha, 朝日新聞社. |year=1994 |isbn=4-02-340052-1 |at=西郷隆盛 |oclc=33014222}} He had six siblings and his younger brother was {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|WD=Q121334120|lt=Marshal-Admiral|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)}} [[:en:Marquis|Marquis]] {{ill|Saigō Jūdō|en|Saigō Jūdō|WD=Q699674|lt=Saigō Jūdō|1=Saigō Jūdō}}. His childhood name was Kokichi and he received the given name Takamori in adulthood. He wrote poetry under the name '''Saigō Nanshū''' (西郷 南洲).Ravina, Mark. ''The Last Samurai: The Life and Battles of Saigō Takamori''. [[:en:John Wiley and Sons|John Wiley and Sons]], 2011. [https://books.google.com/books?id=lwt587Ex_a4C&pg=PT7 Names, Romanizations, and Spelling (page 1 of 2)]. Retrieved from {{ill|Google Books|en|Google Books|WD=Q206033|lt=Google Books|1=Google Books}} on August 7, 2011. {{ISBN|1-118-04556-4}}, {{ISBN|978-1-118-04556-5}}. Shogun [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] resigned, returning power to the Emperor in what came to be known as the [[Meiji Restoration]]. However, Saigō was one of the most vocal and vehement opponents to the negotiated solution, demanding that the Tokugawa be stripped of their lands and special status. His intransigence was one of the major causes of the subsequent {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}. During the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}, Saigō led the imperial forces at the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}}, and afterwards led the imperial army toward Edo, where he accepted the surrender of Edo Castle from {{ill|Katsu Kaishū|en|Katsu Kaishū|WD=Q700470|lt=Katsu Kaishū|1=Katsu Kaishū}}. ==Meiji bureaucrat== [[File:1873_Seikanron_Debate_Saigo_Takamori_Ukiyo-e_by_Suzuki_Toshimoto.png|thumb|left|The {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate. Saigō Takamori is sitting in the center. 1877 woodblock print]] Although {{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|WD=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}} and others were more active and influential in establishing the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Government of Meiji Japan|1=Government of Meiji Japan}}, Saigō retained a key role, and his cooperation was essential in the {{ill|Abolition of the han system|en|Abolition of the han system|WD=Q331905|lt=Abolition of the han system|1=Abolition of the han system}} and the establishment of a conscript army. In 1871 he was left in charge of the caretaker government during the absence of the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}} (1871–73). Saigō initially disagreed with the modernization of Japan and the opening of commerce with the West. He famously opposed the construction of a railway network, insisting that money should rather be spent on military modernization.{{Cite web |url=http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |title=On Saigō and the establishment of a railway |access-date=October 21, 2006 |archive-date=May 27, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527182301/http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |url-status=dead }} Saigō did insist that Japan should go to war with {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}} in the {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate of 1873 due to Korea's refusal to recognize the legitimacy of the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} as head of state of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}, and insulting treatment meted out to Japanese envoys attempting to establish trade and diplomatic relations. At one point, he offered to visit Korea in person and to provoke a ''{{ill|Casus belli|en|Casus belli|WD=Q45635|lt=Casus belli|1=Casus belli}}'' by behaving in such an insulting manner that the Koreans would be forced to kill him.{{Cite book |last=Ravina |first=Mark |title=The last Samurai - The life and Battles of Saigō Takamori |publisher=Wiley Online library |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-471-70537-6 |pages=184}} The other Japanese leaders strongly opposed these plans, partly from budgetary considerations, and partly from realization of the weakness of Japan compared with the western countries from what they had witnessed during the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}}. Saigō resigned from all of his government positions in protest and returned to his hometown of {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}. ==Satsuma Rebellion (1877)== {{Main|Satsuma Rebellion}} [[File:Saigo Takamori Portrait by Tokonami Masayoshi 1887.png|thumb|Portrait of Saigō Takamori as a {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|WD=Q3100832|lt=field marshal|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)}}, faithful depiction by the acquaintance Tokonami Masayoshi in 1887]] [[File:Seinansenso snou.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō preparing for war]] Shortly thereafter, a private military academy known as the {{ill|Shi-gakkō|en|Shi-gakkō|WD=Q11594685|lt=Shi-gakkō|1=Shi-gakkō}} was established in Kagoshima for the faithful ''samurai'' who had also resigned their posts to follow him from Tokyo. These disaffected samurai came to dominate the Kagoshima government, and fearing a rebellion, the government sent warships to Kagoshima to remove weapons from the Kagoshima arsenal. This provoked open conflict, although with the elimination of ''samurai'' rice stipends in 1877, tensions were already extremely high. Although greatly dismayed by the revolt, Saigō was reluctantly persuaded to lead the rebels against the central government. [[File:ShiroyamaBattle.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō Takamori (upper right) directing his troops at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}]] The rebels fought two significant battles against the central government: the {{ill|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|en|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|WD=Q7510168|lt=Siege of Kumamoto Castle|1=Siege of Kumamoto Castle}} and the {{ill|Battle of Tabaruzaka|en|Battle of Tabaruzaka|WD=Q9347968|lt=Battle of Tabaruzaka|1=Battle of Tabaruzaka}}. Saigō was initially confident of his ability to take Kumamoto Castle, but he had underestimated the effectiveness of the imperial conscripts defending the castle. After a failed assault, Saigō settled for a siege. Imperial reinforcements eventually forced their way through the rebel lines at the Battle of Tabaruzaka, ending the siege. The remnants of Saigō's army retreated before the advancing imperials, who whittled it down relentlessly. Eventually Saigō and his final remaining samurai were encircled and annihilated at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}. Saigō's death brought the Satsuma Rebellion to an end. ==Death== [[File:Saigo Takamori Woodblock Print Portrait by Hasegawa Sadanobu II 1877.png|thumb|Woodblock print of Saigō Takamori by Hasegawa Sadanobu II which describes his career, November 1877]] During the battle of Shiroyama, Saigō was badly injured in the hip. The exact manner of his death is unknown. There are no published reports by eyewitnesses. The accounts of his subordinates claim that he stood up and committed ''{{ill|Seppuku|en|Seppuku|WD=Q133462|lt=Seppuku|1=Seppuku}}'' after his injury or that he requested that his friend {{ill|Beppu Shinsuke|en|Beppu Shinsuke|WD=Q937740|lt=Beppu Shinsuke|1=Beppu Shinsuke}} assist his suicide. Three firsthand accounts of the condition of his deceased body exist. It is said that he was shot in the femur, then he thrust a sword into his stomach region, then was decapitated deliberately by a fellow citizen. All three accounts report that the body was decapitated. Two describe a bullet wound to the hip or thigh. As none of the eyewitness accounts mention a wound to the abdomen, or any fresh sword wound at all, it is unknown if Saigō pierced his stomach with his sword.Ravina, Mark J. “The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, Seppuku, and the Politics of Legend.” Journal of Asian Studies 69.3 (2010): 691-721. Some scholars have suggested that neither is the case and that Saigō may have gone into shock following his wound, losing his ability to speak. Several samurai, upon seeing him in this state, would have severed his head, assisting him in the warrior's suicide that they knew he would have wished for. Later, they would have said that he committed ''seppuku'' to preserve his status as a true ''samurai''.{{cite web |url=http://www.emory.edu/EMORY_MAGAZINE/spring2004/precis_samurai.html|title=The Real Last Samurai|publisher=Emory University |website=Emory Magazine|editor=Andrew M. Beierle|access-date=April 10, 2009}} It is not clear what was done with Saigō's head immediately after his death. Some legends say Saigō's manservant hid the head, and it was later found by a government soldier. The head was somehow retrieved by government forces and was reunited with Saigō's body, which was laid next to that of his deputies Kirino and Murata. This was witnessed by the American sea captain John Capen Hubbard. A myth persists that the head was never found. ==Legends== [[File:Saigo Takamori Gunmusho banknote 1877.jpg|thumb|150px|left|Saigō Takamori ''Gunmusho'' (軍務所) banknote, issued in 1877 to finance his war effort. [[:en:Japan Currency Museum|Japan Currency Museum]]]] Multiple legends sprang up concerning Saigō, many of which denied his death. It was believed by some that he had fled to {{ill|Russia|en|Russia|WD=Q159|lt=Russia|1=Russia}}, or ascended to {{ill|Mars|en|Mars|WD=Q111|lt=Mars|1=Mars}}.{{Cite journal|last=RAVINA|first=MARK J.|date=2010|title=The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, "Seppuku", and the Politics of Legend|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40929189|journal=The Journal of Asian Studies|volume=69|issue=3|pages=691–721|doi=10.1017/S0021911810001518|jstor=40929189|s2cid=155001706|issn=0021-9118}} It was even recorded that his image appeared in a comet near the close of the 19th century, an ill omen to his enemies. Unable to overcome the affection that the people had for this paragon of traditional ''samurai'' virtues, the [[:en:Meiji-era|Meiji-era]] government pardoned him posthumously on February 22, 1889. The Japanese people appreciated the fact that he remained loyal to his virtues until his death in 1877. ==Artworks depicting Saigō== [[File:Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku
(Gion, Kyoto, Japan)]] [[File:SaigoTakamori1332.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Saigō Takamori's statue near the southern entrance of Ueno Park.]] [[File:Deathplace of SAIGO Takamori.JPG|thumb|150px|The death place monument at Shiroyama-chō, Kagoshima]] Saigō famously refused to have his photograph taken, but his likeness is now highly visible in Tokyo. A famous bronze statue of Saigō in hunting attire with his dog stands in {{ill|Ueno Park|en|Ueno Park|WD=Q746216|lt=Ueno Park|1=Ueno Park}}, {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}. Made by {{ill|Takamura Kōun|en|Takamura Kōun|WD=Q2080344|lt=Takamura Kōun|1=Takamura Kōun}}, it was unveiled on December 18, 1898. Saigō met the noted British {{ill|Diplomat|en|Diplomat|WD=Q193391|lt=Diplomat|1=Diplomat}} [[:en:Ernest Satow|Ernest Satow]] in the 1860s, as recorded in the latter's ''A Diplomat in Japan'', and Satow was present at the unveiling as recorded in his diary. A reproduction of the same statue stands on {{ill|Okinoerabujima|en|Okinoerabujima|WD=Q94736|lt=Okinoerabujima|1=Okinoerabujima}}, where Saigō had been exiled.{{ill|John Man (author)|en|John Man (author)|WD=Q3431828|lt=Man, John|1=John Man (author)}}. "In the Footsteps of the Real Last Samurai." ''[[:en:School of Oriental and African Studies|SOAS]] World''. 37 (Spring 2011). p30. A Japanese hand fan commemorating the event, which survives in the collection of the Staten Island Historical Society in New York, features a depiction of Saigō Takamori in a scene labeled (in English) "The Battle Near the Citadel of Kumamoto".{{cite web|title=Fan, 1877–1890|url=https://statenisland.pastperfectonline.com/webobject/2BBDFB3D-A583-4BB0-AF0E-163644731340|website=Online Collections Database|publisher=Staten Island Historical Society|access-date=December 2, 2011}} ==Family== ===Ancestry=== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=no |align=center |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1. He was one of the most influential samurai in {{ill|History of Japan|en|History of Japan|WD=Q130436|lt=Japanese history|1=History of Japan}} and one of the {{ill|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|en|Three Great Nobles of the Restoration|WD=Q709678|lt=three great nobles|1=Three Great Nobles of the Restoration}} who led the [[Meiji Restoration]]. Living during the late {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo|1=Edo period}} and early {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}s, he later led the {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|en|Satsuma Rebellion|WD=Q714820|lt=Satsuma Rebellion|1=Satsuma Rebellion}} against the Meiji government. Historian {{ill|Ivan Morris|en|Ivan Morris|WD=Q3826587|lt=Ivan Morris|1=Ivan Morris}} described him as "the quintessential hero of modern Japanese history".{{Cite web|last=Hoffman|first=Michael|date=December 10, 2016|title=Meiji Restoration leader's lessons of sincerity|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2016/12/10/national/history/meiji-restoration-leaders-lessons-sincerity/|url-access=subscription|access-date=June 29, 2021|website=The Japan Times|language=en-US}} ==Early life== '''Saigō Kokichi''' (西郷 小吉) was born in Kajiya, {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|WD=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain|1=Satsuma Domain}}, the eldest son of {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|WD=Q38142|lt=Samurai|1=Samurai}} {{ill|squire|en|squire|WD=Q579516|lt=squire|1=Squire}} (''koshōkumi'') Saigō Kichibē and his wife Masa.{{Cite book |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/33014222 |title=Asashi Nihon rekishi jinbutsu jiten |publisher=Asahi Shinbunsha |others=Asahi Shinbunsha, 朝日新聞社. |year=1994 |isbn=4-02-340052-1 |at=西郷隆盛 |oclc=33014222}} He had six siblings and his younger brother was {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)|WD=Q121334120|lt=Marshal-Admiral|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Navy)}} [[:en:Marquis|Marquis]] {{ill|Saigō Jūdō|en|Saigō Jūdō|WD=Q699674|lt=Saigō Jūdō|1=Saigō Jūdō}}. His childhood name was Kokichi and he received the given name Takamori in adulthood. He wrote poetry under the name '''Saigō Nanshū''' (西郷 南洲).Ravina, Mark. ''The Last Samurai: The Life and Battles of Saigō Takamori''. [[:en:John Wiley and Sons|John Wiley and Sons]], 2011. [https://books.google.com/books?id=lwt587Ex_a4C&pg=PT7 Names, Romanizations, and Spelling (page 1 of 2)]. Retrieved from {{ill|Google Books|en|Google Books|WD=Q206033|lt=Google Books|1=Google Books}} on August 7, 2011. {{ISBN|1-118-04556-4}}, {{ISBN|978-1-118-04556-5}}. Shogun [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] resigned, returning power to the Emperor in what came to be known as the [[Meiji Restoration]]. However, Saigō was one of the most vocal and vehement opponents to the negotiated solution, demanding that the Tokugawa be stripped of their lands and special status. His intransigence was one of the major causes of the subsequent {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}. During the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|WD=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}, Saigō led the imperial forces at the {{ill|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|en|Battle of Toba–Fushimi|WD=Q1193959|lt=Battle of Toba–Fushimi|1=Battle of Toba–Fushimi}}, and afterwards led the imperial army toward Edo, where he accepted the surrender of Edo Castle from {{ill|Katsu Kaishū|en|Katsu Kaishū|WD=Q700470|lt=Katsu Kaishū|1=Katsu Kaishū}}. ==Meiji bureaucrat== [[File:1873_Seikanron_Debate_Saigo_Takamori_Ukiyo-e_by_Suzuki_Toshimoto.png|thumb|left|The {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate. Saigō Takamori is sitting in the center. 1877 woodblock print]] Although {{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|WD=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}} and others were more active and influential in establishing the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Government of Meiji Japan|1=Government of Meiji Japan}}, Saigō retained a key role, and his cooperation was essential in the {{ill|Abolition of the han system|en|Abolition of the han system|WD=Q331905|lt=Abolition of the han system|1=Abolition of the han system}} and the establishment of a conscript army. In 1871 he was left in charge of the caretaker government during the absence of the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}} (1871–73). Saigō initially disagreed with the modernization of Japan and the opening of commerce with the West. He famously opposed the construction of a railway network, insisting that money should rather be spent on military modernization.{{Cite web |url=http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |title=On Saigō and the establishment of a railway |access-date=October 21, 2006 |archive-date=May 27, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527182301/http://www.unu.edu/unupress/unupbooks/uu36je/uu36je0c.htm |url-status=dead }} Saigō did insist that Japan should go to war with {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea|1=Korea}} in the {{ill|Seikanron|en|Seikanron|WD=Q370290|lt=Seikanron|1=Seikanron}} debate of 1873 due to Korea's refusal to recognize the legitimacy of the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|WD=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} as head of state of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|WD=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}, and insulting treatment meted out to Japanese envoys attempting to establish trade and diplomatic relations. At one point, he offered to visit Korea in person and to provoke a ''{{ill|Casus belli|en|Casus belli|WD=Q45635|lt=Casus belli|1=Casus belli}}'' by behaving in such an insulting manner that the Koreans would be forced to kill him.{{Cite book |last=Ravina |first=Mark |title=The last Samurai - The life and Battles of Saigō Takamori |publisher=Wiley Online library |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-471-70537-6 |pages=184}} The other Japanese leaders strongly opposed these plans, partly from budgetary considerations, and partly from realization of the weakness of Japan compared with the western countries from what they had witnessed during the {{ill|Iwakura Mission|en|Iwakura Mission|WD=Q696860|lt=Iwakura Mission|1=Iwakura Mission}}. Saigō resigned from all of his government positions in protest and returned to his hometown of {{ill|Kagoshima|en|Kagoshima|WD=Q15674|lt=Kagoshima|1=Kagoshima}}. ==Satsuma Rebellion (1877)== {{Main|Satsuma Rebellion}} [[File:Saigo Takamori Portrait by Tokonami Masayoshi 1887.png|thumb|Portrait of Saigō Takamori as a {{ill|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|en|Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)|WD=Q3100832|lt=field marshal|1=Gensui (Imperial Japanese Army)}}, faithful depiction by the acquaintance Tokonami Masayoshi in 1887]] [[File:Seinansenso snou.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō preparing for war]] Shortly thereafter, a private military academy known as the {{ill|Shi-gakkō|en|Shi-gakkō|WD=Q11594685|lt=Shi-gakkō|1=Shi-gakkō}} was established in Kagoshima for the faithful ''samurai'' who had also resigned their posts to follow him from Tokyo. These disaffected samurai came to dominate the Kagoshima government, and fearing a rebellion, the government sent warships to Kagoshima to remove weapons from the Kagoshima arsenal. This provoked open conflict, although with the elimination of ''samurai'' rice stipends in 1877, tensions were already extremely high. Although greatly dismayed by the revolt, Saigō was reluctantly persuaded to lead the rebels against the central government. [[File:ShiroyamaBattle.jpg|thumb|left|Saigō Takamori (upper right) directing his troops at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}]] The rebels fought two significant battles against the central government: the {{ill|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|en|Siege of Kumamoto Castle|WD=Q7510168|lt=Siege of Kumamoto Castle|1=Siege of Kumamoto Castle}} and the {{ill|Battle of Tabaruzaka|en|Battle of Tabaruzaka|WD=Q9347968|lt=Battle of Tabaruzaka|1=Battle of Tabaruzaka}}. Saigō was initially confident of his ability to take Kumamoto Castle, but he had underestimated the effectiveness of the imperial conscripts defending the castle. After a failed assault, Saigō settled for a siege. Imperial reinforcements eventually forced their way through the rebel lines at the Battle of Tabaruzaka, ending the siege. The remnants of Saigō's army retreated before the advancing imperials, who whittled it down relentlessly. Eventually Saigō and his final remaining samurai were encircled and annihilated at the {{ill|Battle of Shiroyama|en|Battle of Shiroyama|WD=Q1788393|lt=Battle of Shiroyama|1=Battle of Shiroyama}}. Saigō's death brought the Satsuma Rebellion to an end. ==Death== [[File:Saigo Takamori Woodblock Print Portrait by Hasegawa Sadanobu II 1877.png|thumb|Woodblock print of Saigō Takamori by Hasegawa Sadanobu II which describes his career, November 1877]] During the battle of Shiroyama, Saigō was badly injured in the hip. The exact manner of his death is unknown. There are no published reports by eyewitnesses. The accounts of his subordinates claim that he stood up and committed ''{{ill|Seppuku|en|Seppuku|WD=Q133462|lt=Seppuku|1=Seppuku}}'' after his injury or that he requested that his friend {{ill|Beppu Shinsuke|en|Beppu Shinsuke|WD=Q937740|lt=Beppu Shinsuke|1=Beppu Shinsuke}} assist his suicide. Three firsthand accounts of the condition of his deceased body exist. It is said that he was shot in the femur, then he thrust a sword into his stomach region, then was decapitated deliberately by a fellow citizen. All three accounts report that the body was decapitated. Two describe a bullet wound to the hip or thigh. As none of the eyewitness accounts mention a wound to the abdomen, or any fresh sword wound at all, it is unknown if Saigō pierced his stomach with his sword.Ravina, Mark J. “The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, Seppuku, and the Politics of Legend.” Journal of Asian Studies 69.3 (2010): 691-721. Some scholars have suggested that neither is the case and that Saigō may have gone into shock following his wound, losing his ability to speak. Several samurai, upon seeing him in this state, would have severed his head, assisting him in the warrior's suicide that they knew he would have wished for. Later, they would have said that he committed ''seppuku'' to preserve his status as a true ''samurai''.{{cite web |url=http://www.emory.edu/EMORY_MAGAZINE/spring2004/precis_samurai.html|title=The Real Last Samurai|publisher=Emory University |website=Emory Magazine|editor=Andrew M. Beierle|access-date=April 10, 2009}} It is not clear what was done with Saigō's head immediately after his death. Some legends say Saigō's manservant hid the head, and it was later found by a government soldier. The head was somehow retrieved by government forces and was reunited with Saigō's body, which was laid next to that of his deputies Kirino and Murata. This was witnessed by the American sea captain John Capen Hubbard. A myth persists that the head was never found. ==Legends== [[File:Saigo Takamori Gunmusho banknote 1877.jpg|thumb|150px|left|Saigō Takamori ''Gunmusho'' (軍務所) banknote, issued in 1877 to finance his war effort. [[:en:Japan Currency Museum|Japan Currency Museum]]]] Multiple legends sprang up concerning Saigō, many of which denied his death. It was believed by some that he had fled to {{ill|Russia|en|Russia|WD=Q159|lt=Russia|1=Russia}}, or ascended to {{ill|Mars|en|Mars|WD=Q111|lt=Mars|1=Mars}}.{{Cite journal|last=RAVINA|first=MARK J.|date=2010|title=The Apocryphal Suicide of Saigō Takamori: Samurai, "Seppuku", and the Politics of Legend|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40929189|journal=The Journal of Asian Studies|volume=69|issue=3|pages=691–721|doi=10.1017/S0021911810001518|jstor=40929189|s2cid=155001706|issn=0021-9118}} It was even recorded that his image appeared in a comet near the close of the 19th century, an ill omen to his enemies. Unable to overcome the affection that the people had for this paragon of traditional ''samurai'' virtues, the [[:en:Meiji-era|Meiji-era]] government pardoned him posthumously on February 22, 1889. The Japanese people appreciated the fact that he remained loyal to his virtues until his death in 1877. ==Artworks depicting Saigō== [[File:Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Monument of Satsu Do Toubaku no Mitsuyaku
(Gion, Kyoto, Japan)]] [[File:SaigoTakamori1332.jpg|thumb|right|150px|Saigō Takamori's statue near the southern entrance of Ueno Park.]] [[File:Deathplace of SAIGO Takamori.JPG|thumb|150px|The death place monument at Shiroyama-chō, Kagoshima]] Saigō famously refused to have his photograph taken, but his likeness is now highly visible in Tokyo. A famous bronze statue of Saigō in hunting attire with his dog stands in {{ill|Ueno Park|en|Ueno Park|WD=Q746216|lt=Ueno Park|1=Ueno Park}}, {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}. Made by {{ill|Takamura Kōun|en|Takamura Kōun|WD=Q2080344|lt=Takamura Kōun|1=Takamura Kōun}}, it was unveiled on December 18, 1898. Saigō met the noted British {{ill|Diplomat|en|Diplomat|WD=Q193391|lt=Diplomat|1=Diplomat}} [[:en:Ernest Satow|Ernest Satow]] in the 1860s, as recorded in the latter's ''A Diplomat in Japan'', and Satow was present at the unveiling as recorded in his diary. A reproduction of the same statue stands on {{ill|Okinoerabujima|en|Okinoerabujima|WD=Q94736|lt=Okinoerabujima|1=Okinoerabujima}}, where Saigō had been exiled.{{ill|John Man (author)|en|John Man (author)|WD=Q3431828|lt=Man, John|1=John Man (author)}}. "In the Footsteps of the Real Last Samurai." ''[[:en:School of Oriental and African Studies|SOAS]] World''. 37 (Spring 2011). p30. A Japanese hand fan commemorating the event, which survives in the collection of the Staten Island Historical Society in New York, features a depiction of Saigō Takamori in a scene labeled (in English) "The Battle Near the Citadel of Kumamoto".{{cite web|title=Fan, 1877–1890|url=https://statenisland.pastperfectonline.com/webobject/2BBDFB3D-A583-4BB0-AF0E-163644731340|website=Online Collections Database|publisher=Staten Island Historical Society|access-date=December 2, 2011}} ==Family== ===Ancestry=== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=no |align=center |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1.
